facts.claim: Ryan Kickland's "In Trouble" is track 11 on Justified (Music from the Original Television Series), released by Madison Gate Records on January 8, 2013.
The track runs 2:59 and is credited to Ryan Kickland as main artist on a 13-track, roughly 51-minute compilation.
Discogs credits Ryan Kickland as the writer of "In Trouble".
Kickland describes "In Trouble" as a 2012 single that was featured on the FX series Justified.
The Justified soundtrack's executive producer was Greg Sill.

Film Music Reporter described the album as FX's Justified soundtrack from Madison Gate Records, with other artists including Gangstagrass, Dave Alvin, Beverley Staunton, Lynda Kay and Robert J. Walsh.
Kickland is a Black Hills, South Dakota singer-songwriter whose music has a lonely, heartbroken tone and tells stories about characters from the dark side of the tracks.
By 2013 Kickland had released nine albums, the most recent being 2011's "Songs to Stare Wildly By", and his songs had been featured on Justified.

SDPB's Steve Zwemke interviewed Kickland on January 24, 2013, shortly after the soundtrack's release; the interview aired after a concert recorded September 21, 2012 at the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City.

Kickland was vocalist, guitarist and songwriter in the psychedelic/fusion rock band Animalcule, which disbanded in 2006. He began releasing solo folk recordings around 2001 and is best known for folk/Americana.
Kickland makes music for television and film in his home studio, and released the album Special Magic in May 2017.

research.lineage: Kickland's song sits in the folk/Americana singer-songwriter tradition of stark, story-driven, dark-side-of-the-tracks narratives, which suited the country and roots-leaning Justified soundtrack.

draft:
The trick of **In Trouble** lives in one small word. Each chorus states the problem twice, and the first time Ryan Kickland follows it with "And it's where I belong," a shrug, almost a boast. The second time the "and" becomes a "but," and the shrug turns into a confession. Same melody, same lines, one conjunction apart, and the song keeps flipping between those two readings until you can't say which one the narrator believes.

That push and pull is the whole emotional engine. This is someone who has burned the bridge home ("There ain't no road that can lead me home") and decided to call it a choice. When someone offers comfort, the answer is a flat refusal: "I don't need your shelter babe." The pride is real, but so is the howling wind in the first line, and the loneliness doesn't go away just because the narrator won't name it. The third verse is where the act slips. Darkness is "spreading all across my skin," and then the narrator admits not knowing "where I end and where my shadow begin." It's the most frightening line in the song because it's the least defiant. The trouble isn't a place anymore. It's become part of who this person is.

The arrangement doesn't comment on any of this. It just keeps walking. A fingerpicked guitar rolls through arpeggios over a walking bass line, and the drums hold a plain, steady beat with the snare on two and four. The tempo sits in the middle, unhurried. Kickland's voice is clear and mid-range, sung straight, with a little rawness left in. A second voice comes in with harmony above the lead, so the claim of belonging gets sung by two people, which makes it sound less lonely than it is. The room is dry and close, nothing dressed up. Between verses, the lyric drops into a run of wordless "ah"s, as if the narrator has run out of ways to explain.

Kickland writes from the Black Hills of South Dakota, in the folk and Americana singer-songwriter tradition of stark stories about people from the wrong side of the tracks. Before going solo, he fronted the psychedelic rock band Animalcule. He wrote this one himself and released it as a 2012 single. It was featured on FX's *Justified*, then landed as track 11 on the show's soundtrack from Madison Gate Records, alongside Gangstagrass and Dave Alvin. It fits there easily. *Justified* was full of people who mistook their worst habits for home.

The song sticks because it lets you sing along with a defiance you can hear cracking, and somewhere between the "and" and the "but," you start to feel what it costs to believe you belong in the dark.
